title: Perceptions of lighting, perceived restorativeness, preference and fear in outdoor spaces
review_question: To explore whether lighting is connected with the perception of the restorative potential of night-time environments, and how different lighting attributes affect perceptions of pleasant and safe lighting environments, providing practical suggestions for lighting implementations.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The literature review focuses on environmental psychology, lighting design, urban planning, and lighting technology, specifically related to restoration, preference, and fear in outdoor nightscapes. The thesis itself comprises four original studies (I, II, III, IV) investigating these relationships.

synthesis_conclusions: Natural environments have restorative effects, generally yielding more positive health outcomes than urban ones, including short-term stress/mental fatigue recovery, faster physical recovery from illness, and long-term well-being.

The perceived quality of the lighting environment, including the focus of light and colour quality, correlates with the perception of restorative potential, preference, and safety in night-time environments.

Focusing light on natural or pleasant scene contents promotes perceived restorativeness, preference, and safety, while focusing on urban or unpleasant contents has a hampering effect on restorativeness.
Perceived brightness can be experienced both positively and negatively; excessive brightness may be linked to negative experiences and hinder attentional recovery.
Lighting interventions should adopt quality-based approaches and consider lighting expectations related to different functions, rather than solely increasing illuminance levels.
Near-home lighting environments should be viewed as potential settings for pleasurable recreational activities and restoration, not merely as places to reduce fear and insecurity.
evidence_gaps: Lack of studies on mixed urban-natural environments in restoration research.
Restoration research has predominantly focused on daytime environments; nightscapes and other contexts require more attention.
Need to incorporate soundscapes, smells, and tactile sensations into restoration research, moving beyond visual exposure.
Further theoretical development of restoration theories is needed.
Urban lightscape studies have concentrated on fear in urban streets, with other factors and contexts receiving minor attention.
Lighting conditions in fear studies are often weakly documented, hindering the identification of effective lighting attributes.
Demand for night-time visual appraisal studies that do not solely focus on fear of crime.
Lack of research describing people’s lighting expectations in relation to different contexts, particularly regarding spectral distribution and brightness preferences in outdoor lighting environments.
Need for more scenes, scene types, and field experiments to validate suggested connections between lighting and environmental perceptions.
Need for more research scoring only positive factors in lighting preference research on urban nightscapes.
Further exploration of the connections between restoration/preference and brightness, especially concerning excessive brightness.
Validation is needed for the indication that dim, warm lighting is perceived as natural in suburban pedestrian environments.
The possible effects of lighting on restoration at a behavioural and/or physiological level need to be studied with targeted research.
More versatility is needed in study areas for night-time restoration, beyond suburban contexts.
Research is needed on whether lighting affects aggressive behaviour through the recovery of directed attention.
Investigation into the involvement of ART's 'being away' component in the relationship between spectral power distribution, mood, and cognitive performance.
Research on whether restoration during evening benefits good sleep.
Understanding perceived brightness and spectral power distribution expectations related to different outdoor functions.
Further research is needed to compare results with other response scales beyond the commonly used 7-point Likert scale.
heterogeneity_sources: Variations in preliminary lighting conditions, follow-up times, characteristics of residents, halo effects, and the complex nature of reactions in lighting intervention studies.
Differences in lighting design application (e.g., non-uniform lighting contradicting physical structures vs. emphasizing them) may explain contradictory results regarding uniformity and safety.
limitations: Research is limited to perceived restorativeness, with behavioural and/or physiological restoration not studied.

Small sample of settings limits generalizability to all scene contents and environmental contexts; low number of scenes harms reliability, especially for explorative field studies 3 and 4 due to confounded factors.
Studies 1 and 2 used simulations instead of real environments, and the Lightscape simulations were considered coarse at the time, potentially affecting validity.
Studies 1 and 2 were conducted during daytime, despite representing night-time environments, which may have affected results.
Single-item scales were used in studies 3 and 4 to limit evaluation time, potentially harming reliability.
Studies 3 and 4 used local residents, introducing a potential source of bias.
Participants in studies 3 and 4 were aware of the study purpose, potentially leading to stronger emphasis on lighting effects.
Cultural aspects were not fully explored, and lighting preferences may differ due to cultural reasons.
Results may differ in different climate zones, as outdoor lighting use in Finland is mainly restricted to colder seasons and perceptions of colour temperature are connected to ambient temperature.
Nonlinear brightness and extensiveness scales may have confused participants.
The salience of the stimuli used was a limitation; real environment experiments with eye-tracking and luminance measurements would provide more understanding.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue.
